title: Sinking Spring to Oak Ridge: the Rail-Splitter, the Greenbacks, and the Long Train Home
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Sinking Spring Farm, the one-room cabin
stops.date_confidence: attested to 12 February 1809. The county is corrected: the farm lay in Hardin County in 1809; LaRue was carved out of Hardin only in 1843, and both Wikipedia and the NPS give the modern county. Coordinate from the NPS birthplace park.
stops.campa: Thomas Lincoln, carpenter and farmer, holds land on the South Fork of Nolin Creek, land whose title will not survive the lawyers. In a one-room cabin of unsquared logs his wife Nancy Hanks bears a son on a February morning and they name him Abraham, after Thomas's father. The county is Hardin; a later generation will carve LaRue out of it and draw the new line around this cabin. The farm is called Sinking Spring for the cold water that comes out of the limestone below the door and goes back into the rock a few yards on.
suggested_refs: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park, Hodgenville, Kentucky
sources: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park (NPS)

stops.name: Little Pigeon Creek, the crossing into Indiana
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1816; month and day default to 01. The source says the family moved 'reportedly over disputed land titles' and hedges the motive itself. The coordinate is the Lincoln Boyhood National Memorial site and is not given in the research pool.
stops.campa: The Kentucky titles fail, as titles surveyed by landmark and pace tend to fail, and Thomas Lincoln loses ground twice to men with better paper. He crosses the Ohio into Indiana, free soil under the Northwest Ordinance, and takes a quarter section at Little Pigeon Creek where the survey is federal and the lines hold. The boy is seven. He helps clear the ground with an axe and keeps the habit, and forty-four years later the men who nominate him will hand out fence rails as campaign material and call him a rail-splitter, and the story will be true.
suggested_refs: Lincoln Boyhood National Memorial, Spencer County, Indiana

stops.name: Little Pigeon Creek, the milk sickness and the second mother
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 October 1818 for the death and 2 December 1819 for the remarriage. The schooling figure named in this campa is retagged [R]: no attendance records survive, the source formulation is 'less than 12 months by age 15' rather than an event, and the pool's own note concedes it is only commonly cited.
stops.campa: White snakeroot grows in the shaded woods and the cattle eat it, and the poison comes through in the milk. Nancy Hanks Lincoln sickens in the autumn and dies, and the boy of nine helps his father cut the pegs for her coffin. Thomas rides back to Kentucky and returns fourteen months later with Sarah Bush Johnston, a widow with three children and a wagonload of furniture. She finds the two Lincoln children half-wild and puts books in front of the boy. His formal schooling will add up to less than a year in total. The reading does not stop.
suggested_refs: The grave of Nancy Hanks Lincoln, Lincoln Boyhood National Memorial

stops.name: Little Pigeon Creek, Sarah dead in childbirth
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 January 1828. The burial place and the subsequent estrangement between the Lincoln and Grigsby families are standard secondary detail, not in the research pool. The melancholy described at the end of the campa is [R]: it descends from the Herndon-Weik informant testimony, which was not consulted here, and no source dates its onset.
stops.campa: His sister Sarah, two years older, the one who kept the house after their mother died, marries Aaron Grigsby and dies in childbirth with the baby. Lincoln is nineteen. The Grigsbys bury her in the churchyard, and the friendship between the two families does not recover. He has now buried a mother and a sister in the same clearing. The men who know him in Illinois will describe a settled melancholy in him, and not one of them will be able to say when it started.
suggested_refs: The grave of Sarah Lincoln Grigsby, Little Pigeon Baptist churchyard

segments.name: New Salem and the Prairie Legislature

stops.name: Macon County, the family crosses into Illinois
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1830; day defaults to 01. Coordinate is Decatur, the nearest fixed point to the Sangamon River site, and is not given in the research pool.
stops.campa: The family moves again, ox-wagons west across the Wabash into Illinois, to a site on the north bank of the Sangamon in Macon County. Lincoln is twenty-one, of age, and this is the last move he makes as his father's son. He splits the rails for the new fence, breaks the prairie sod for one season, and then walks away from farming for good. He will not attend his father's funeral thirty-one years later, and he leaves no explanation of that anywhere his secretaries or his law partner could find.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln Trail Homestead site on the Sangamon, Macon County, Illinois

stops.name: New Salem, clerk in the general store
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1831; month and day default to 01. The Denton Offutt flatboat voyage to New Orleans is standard secondary detail, not in the research pool. Coordinate is the reconstructed village of Lincoln's New Salem.
stops.campa: He hires on to take a flatboat of cargo down to New Orleans, and then to clerk in the store his employer means to open at New Salem, a village of a hundred souls on a bluff over the Sangamon with a milldam across it. Lincoln arrives with nothing, six feet four inches of him, and reads everything the village owns. He keeps the accounts honestly enough that the town remarks on it, and learns surveying and grammar from whoever will sit down and teach him.
suggested_refs: Lincoln's New Salem State Historic Site, Menard County, Illinois

stops.name: New Salem, captain of volunteers and a first defeat
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1832 for both the militia service and the first candidacy; month and day default to 01. That he saw no combat in the Black Hawk War is standard secondary detail, not in the pool.
stops.campa: Black Hawk crosses the Mississippi with his band and Illinois calls for volunteers. The New Salem company elects Lincoln its captain, the first office of any kind he holds, and he serves out the summer without meeting the enemy in the field. In the same year he stands for the state legislature and is beaten. He is twenty-three, with no trade and no capital, and the store he clerks in is closing. The men who elected him captain had known him one year.
suggested_refs: The Black Hawk War muster rolls of the Illinois volunteers, 1832

stops.name: New Salem, the store that fails
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1833; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He buys into the Lincoln-Berry store with William Berry, on credit, in a village whose trade is already draining off to the towns with better landings. The store fails. Berry dies and the whole debt lands on the surviving partner, who calls it the national debt and spends most of a decade paying it off out of a lawyer's fees. He owes, on paper, to men entitled to it, more money than he can see his way to. He is a legislator and a licensed lawyer for years before he is out from under it.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed Lincoln-Berry store, Lincoln's New Salem

stops.name: Vandalia, elected to the Illinois House
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1834 for the election; month and day default to 01. The pin is Vandalia, the state capital and seat of the legislature until the 1839 removal to Springfield, which the pool does not state; the coordinate is not in the pool.
stops.campa: The second attempt succeeds. Sangamon County sends him to the Illinois House of Representatives and he rides to the state capital at Vandalia, a Whig for banks, roads, canals, and internal improvement generally, in a state that has almost none of them. He serves four consecutive terms, through 1842, and learns the arithmetic of a legislature: who can be traded with, and how many men have to want a thing before it happens. Vandalia is a town of a few hundred people and a brick statehouse, and it is the largest political room he has yet stood in.
suggested_refs: The Vandalia State House, seat of the Illinois legislature to 1839

stops.name: Springfield, admitted to the bar
stops.date_confidence: attested to 9 September 1836. Circuit riding and the 1844 Herndon partnership are attested in the pool for the practice and the year respectively; the description of the circuit itself is standard secondary detail.
stops.campa: On the ninth of September he is licensed to practice law in Illinois, having read borrowed books and never seen the inside of a law school. He rides the judicial circuit of central Illinois twice a year, sleeping two to a bed in county-seat taverns, arguing mortgage and slander and debt and murder in front of the same juries and the same handful of lawyers. In 1844 he takes a junior partner, William Herndon, whose name stays on the door for the rest of his life and who will spend his own old age collecting everything anyone in Illinois can still remember about him.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln-Herndon Law Offices, Springfield, Illinois

segments.name: Springfield: the Law, the House, the Graves

stops.name: Springfield, the Lyceum address
stops.date_confidence: attested to 27 January 1838. The research pool supplies no verified text of the address, so the campa paraphrases it and no quote field is carried; the phrase about a political religion is genuinely Lincoln's but is not quoted here for that reason.
stops.campa: Twenty-eight years old, he stands up before the Young Men's Lyceum of Springfield and tells a room of young men that the danger to the republic will not arrive from abroad. It will come from mob law, from citizens who decide the courts are slower than their own judgment, and from some future man of towering ambition who finds a country already in the habit of ignoring its own rules. He asks them to make reverence for the laws into something like a political religion. He is a country lawyer two years at the bar, and twenty-seven years from Ford's Theatre.
suggested_refs: The Lyceum Address, Springfield, 27 January 1838

stops.name: Springfield, the marriage to Mary Todd
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 November 1842. Robert's birth is attested to 1843 without month or day; Eddie 1846, Willie 21 December 1850, Tad 4 April 1853.
stops.campa: He marries Mary Todd in her sister's parlor in Springfield, a Kentucky banker's daughter with French and a temper of her own, courted and broken off with and courted again across three years. Robert is born the next year, the only one of four sons who will reach manhood; Edward follows in 1846, William in 1850, Thomas in 1853. She has married a man with no money, one suit, and a habit of stretching out on the office floor to read the newspapers aloud, and she has decided that he will be president.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln Home National Historic Site, Eighth and Jackson, Springfield

stops.name: Washington, one term in the House
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1847 for the term; month and day default to 01. The Thirtieth Congress sat from December 1847. The Spot Resolutions and his Mexican War opposition are absent from the research pool and are not asserted.
stops.campa: Illinois's seventh district sends him to Washington for a single term in the House of Representatives. He is one Whig in a chamber occupied by a war with Mexico and by the question of whether slavery will follow the flag into whatever the war takes. He makes no mark that anyone outside Illinois notices. He does not stand again, goes home to the circuit, and spends the next five years as a lawyer finished with politics, which is what he tells people and appears at the time to believe.
suggested_refs: The old House chamber, now Statuary Hall, United States Capitol

stops.name: Springfield, Eddie's grave and the two sons after
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 February 1850 for Eddie's death, 21 December 1850 for Willie's birth and 4 April 1853 for Tad's. That three of the four sons predecease their mother rests on Tad's death in 1871 and Mary's in 1882, neither of which is in the research pool.
stops.campa: Edward Baker Lincoln dies in the Springfield house a month short of four years old, and Mary does not leave her room. Ten months later William Wallace is born, and two years after that Thomas, called Tad. Three of the four sons will be dead before their mother is. The house fills up again behind the grave, which in Springfield in 1850 is ordinary arithmetic, and the mother in the upstairs room is not consoled by how ordinary it is. Lincoln is forty-one, prosperous, locally famous, and out of public life.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln plot, Oak Ridge Cemetery, Springfield

stops.name: Peoria, against the extension
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1854 for the Kansas-Nebraska Act and October 1854 for the Peoria speech; day defaults to 01. The three-hour duration and the pairing against Douglas the same evening are standard secondary detail, not in the pool.
stops.campa: In May Congress passes the Kansas-Nebraska Act, repeals the old line, and hands the question of slavery in the territories to whoever settles them first. Lincoln, five years out of politics, comes back. At Peoria in October he speaks for three hours against the extension of slavery into the territories, following Stephen Douglas, who has just spoken for three hours in favor. He does not call for abolition where slavery already stands. He says the thing must not be allowed to spread, and that a self-governing people cannot govern another people without their consent.
suggested_refs: The Peoria speech of 16 October 1854, printed at length in the Illinois press

stops.name: Ottawa, the first of seven debates
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1858 for the campaign and the seven debates; the research pool gives no individual dates or sites, so month and day default to 01 and the pin is Ottawa, the first debate site. Debate format, crowd figures and the 1860 Ohio book edition of the transcripts are standard secondary detail, not in the pool. His 1856 entry into the forming Republican Party is attested to that year.
stops.campa: Two years after joining the new Republican Party he goes at Douglas for the Senate seat. They meet seven times in seven congressional districts, three hours a debate in the open air, before crowds of ten and twelve thousand who stand in the sun to hear it. The transcripts run in papers across the country. Democrats keep the Illinois legislature, and the legislature returns Douglas to Washington. Lincoln loses the seat. Two years later an Ohio house prints the transcripts as a book, and the men choosing a presidential candidate have read them.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln-Douglas debate site at Washington Square, Ottawa, Illinois

stops.name: Cooper Union, the speech that makes him national
stops.date_confidence: attested to 27 February 1860. The Brady photograph taken the same day, the audience figure and the Brooklyn origin of the invitation are standard secondary detail, not in the research pool.
stops.campa: He comes east at the invitation of a Brooklyn church, is moved to the Cooper Institute in Manhattan, and stands in a new suit before an audience that has come to look at the prairie curiosity. He argues history rather than passion: that a majority of the framers who signed the Constitution voted to restrict slavery in federal territory, and that the Republicans therefore hold the older ground. Mathew Brady photographs him the same day. The speech and the photograph together are what the nominating convention sees three months later.
suggested_refs: The Great Hall of the Cooper Union, Manhattan

stops.name: Washington, the rifle sent to Damascus
stops.date_confidence: contested. The atlas dates this gift to September 1860 in abdelkader.journey.json, but Lincoln was then a private citizen, neither president nor president-elect. Either the gift is later, the honors having arrived over many months, or the attribution is loose for a gift from the United States government. Pin inherited byte-identical from the abdelkader interlock; nothing reached resolves the date.
stops.campa: In July the Christian quarter of Damascus burns, and the Emir Abdelkader, the exiled Algerian, arms his household and pulls thousands of strangers out of the fire. The courts of Europe answer with medals, swords, and rifles, and among them, from Washington, a gold-inlaid rifle sent in Lincoln's name. The two men never meet. One is a defeated commander living on a French pension in an Ottoman city; the other is an Illinois lawyer about to be elected to preside over a war of his own. The atlas records this gift at the Damascus end, and here.
suggested_refs: The gold-inlaid rifle presented to Emir Abdelkader, among the honors of 1860

stops.name: Springfield, elected sixteenth president
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1860; day defaults to 01. The vote share, the four-way split and the states where he was not on the ballot are standard secondary detail, not in the research pool.
stops.campa: Four candidates split the country and he takes it with well under half the popular vote and no votes at all in the states where he is not on the ballot. He carries the free states and wins the electoral college outright. He learns the returns in the Springfield telegraph office and walks home to tell his wife. Before he is sworn in, seven states will have declared themselves out of the Union, and the presidency he has just won will be smaller by a third of its territory on the day he takes the oath.
suggested_refs: The Springfield telegraph office where the 1860 returns came in

stops.name: The Capitol, the first inauguration
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 March 1861. The unfinished dome, the guard posted by Winfield Scott and the text of the First Inaugural are standard secondary detail; the research pool supplies no inaugural text, so the campa paraphrases and carries no quote.
stops.campa: He takes the oath on the east front of an unfinished Capitol, the dome open to the sky and scaffolded, under a heavy guard of regulars posted against a rumored assassination. Seven states have already gone out and formed a government at Montgomery. He tells the seceded South that the government will hold and occupy what belongs to it, that there need be no bloodshed unless it is forced upon the national authority, and that memory itself will pull the country back together. Five weeks later Fort Sumter is fired on.
suggested_refs: The First Inaugural Address, 4 March 1861

stops.name: The White House, the writ suspended
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1861 for the suspension; the research pool gives the month only and the day defaults to 01. The Baltimore riots, Ex parte Merryman and Taney's circuit ruling are standard secondary detail, not in the pool.
stops.campa: With mobs cutting the rail line and Washington briefly isolated from the North, he suspends the writ of habeas corpus along the military line to the capital, and later in wider districts. The Constitution permits suspension in cases of rebellion but puts the clause in the article describing the powers of Congress, and Congress is not sitting. The Chief Justice, riding circuit, rules against him and is ignored. Lincoln asks whether all the laws but one are to go unexecuted, and the government itself go to pieces, lest that one be violated.
suggested_refs: The proclamation suspending the writ along the Philadelphia to Washington line

stops.name: The White House, Willie dead of typhoid
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 February 1862. Tad's simultaneous illness and recovery, and the cancellation of the Marine Band's summer concerts, are standard secondary detail, not in the research pool. Pin inherited byte-identical from the atlas's White House coordinate.
stops.campa: Typhoid comes up out of the Potomac and the White House cisterns, and William Wallace Lincoln, eleven years old, dies in an upstairs bedroom in February while his father is directing a war. Mary collapses and does not enter the room again. Tad, sick in the same weeks, lives. It is the second son the Lincolns have buried and the first they have buried in this house. The Marine Band's summer concerts on the White House lawn are cancelled for the season.
suggested_refs: The Prince of Wales Room, White House, where Willie Lincoln died

stops.name: The White House, the Emancipation Proclamation
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 January 1863 for the final proclamation and to September 1862 for the preliminary one, the research pool giving the month only for the latter rather than the canonical 22 September. The New Year's reception and the remark about his shaking hand are standard secondary detail.
stops.campa: After Antietam in September he issues the warning: any state still in rebellion on the first of January will have its slaves declared free. No state comes back. On New Year's Day he shakes hands for three hours at the public reception, then goes upstairs and signs, and remarks that his arm is nearly paralyzed and that if his signature wavers everyone will say he hesitated. The proclamation frees no one in the loyal border states and reaches no one the armies have not reached. It is a war measure, and it turns every mile the army takes into an instrument of it.
suggested_refs: The Emancipation Proclamation, 1 January 1863, National Archives

stops.name: Gettysburg, the Soldiers' National Cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested to 19 November 1863. The research pool supplies no verified text of the address, so the campa describes what it does rather than quoting it. Everett's two hours and the hostile press notices are standard secondary detail.
stops.campa: Four and a half months after the battle he comes up to dedicate the cemetery where the Union dead are being reburied. Edward Everett speaks for two hours; Lincoln speaks for two or three minutes and sits down, and some of the papers say he failed. He does not mention slavery, the South, or a single general. He puts the country's founding four score and seven years back, at the Declaration rather than the Constitution, and makes the dead into the argument: the living finish what the dead began, or the dead are wasted.
suggested_refs: The Soldiers' National Cemetery, Gettysburg, Pennsylvania

segments.name: The Money of a Country at War

stops.name: Washington, the Demand Notes and the green ink
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1861 for the Demand Notes, approximately fifty million dollars authorized, and to December 1861 for the suspension of specie payments; the research pool gives months only and days default to 01. The Bakunin landfall is attested in mikhail_bakunin.journey.json to 15 October 1861.
stops.campa: The war outruns the Treasury's revenue within weeks, and the government has no paper money of its own to pay with. In July Congress authorizes Demand Notes, some fifty million dollars of them, printed with green ink on the reverse, which is the entire reason anyone ever calls them greenbacks. In December the banks suspend payment in gold and silver, and the notes become, by default, the money there is. That October Mikhail Bakunin, escaped from Siberia by way of Japan, comes ashore at San Francisco into a country six months into the war that is printing them.
suggested_refs: Surviving Demand Notes of 1861, the first federal paper money since the Revolution

stops.name: The White House, the First Legal Tender Act
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 February 1862. Sources disagree on the amount: the pool carries $150 million as authorized, and notes that the figure appears elsewhere as $60 million in a first tranche on Chase's own account. Not adjudicated. Franklin's 1729 pamphlet is attested in benjamin_franklin.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of February he signs the Legal Tender Act: a hundred and fifty million dollars in United States Notes, bearing no interest, redeemable in nothing, and good by statute for nearly every public and private debt in the country. It is the first federal money that is money because the law says so. Benjamin Franklin had printed colonial bills a hundred and thirty-three years earlier and argued in a pamphlet that paper backed by a government's credit is a currency like any other. The Treasury now does it at national scale, to pay an army.
stops.quote: The judicious legislation of Congress, securing the receivability of these notes for loans and internal duties and making them a legal tender for other debts, has made them an universal currency.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Lincoln, Second Annual Message to Congress, 1 December 1862, looking back on the February act
suggested_refs: The Legal Tender Act of 25 February 1862, U.S. Statutes at Large, 37th Congress

stops.name: Washington, the second act and the Secretary's own face
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1862 for the second act, month only, day defaults to 01. The Chase portrait on the $1 United States Note, Series 1862-63, engraved by Joseph P. Ourdan, is attested; the pool's claim that he is the only Treasury official ever on that denomination is unsourced and has been dropped. Chase's 1864 candidacy is standard secondary detail.
stops.campa: A second act in July authorizes another issue, because the first is already spent. The one-dollar note of the series carries the portrait of Salmon P. Chase, Secretary of the Treasury, engraved by Joseph Ourdan: the man who designed the currency, printed on the smallest denomination of it, at a moment when he is quietly seeking the presidency from the man who appointed him. Chase's face is in every pocket in the Union before his name is on a single ballot. He will not get the nomination, and Lincoln will make him Chief Justice anyway.
suggested_refs: The $1 United States Note, Series 1862-63, with Chase's portrait

stops.name: The Capitol, the Second Annual Message
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 December 1862 for the message and to December 1862 for the gold premium of roughly 29 percent.
stops.campa: He goes up to Congress with the year's accounting. Gold now commands a premium of about twenty-nine percent over the paper, which is to say the dollar he made legal tender in February buys seventy-seven cents of the metal it replaced. He does not disown the notes. He explains them as a thing the banks forced on the government, and then asks Congress for the next step: banking associations chartered under a general act, issuing notes secured by federal bonds. This is the same message that ends by telling them they cannot escape history.
stops.quote: The suspension of specie payments by the banks soon after the commencement of your last session made large issues of United States notes unavoidable.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Lincoln, Second Annual Message to Congress, 1 December 1862 (Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The Second Annual Message to Congress, 1 December 1862
sources: Abraham Lincoln, Second Annual Message to Congress, 1 December 1862 (Wikisource)

stops.name: The White House, the National Banking Act
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 February 1863; a third Legal Tender Act follows in March 1863, month only in the pool. The Jackson material is attested in andrew_jackson.journey.json for 1832 and 1833; the causal line forward to 1863 is a reconstruction, an inference that file does not draw.
stops.campa: He signs the National Currency Act: federally chartered banks, required to hold at least a third of their capital in United States bonds, empowered to issue a uniform national currency against them, supervised by a new Comptroller of the Currency inside the Treasury. A third Legal Tender Act follows in March. Thirty years earlier Andrew Jackson had killed the Second Bank of the United States and scattered the federal deposits into state banks, leaving the country a thousand kinds of paper and no national money at all. This act fills the hole Jackson made, and pays for the war with the same instrument.
stops.quote: I know of none which promises so certain results and is at the same time so unobjectionable as the organization of banking associations, under a general act of Congress, well guarded in its provisions. To such associations the Government might furnish circulating notes, on the security of United States bonds deposited in the Treasury.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Lincoln, Second Annual Message to Congress, 1 December 1862, two consecutive sentences proposing what became this act
suggested_refs: The National Currency Act of 25 February 1863, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
sources: Abraham Lincoln, Second Annual Message to Congress, 1 December 1862 (Wikisource)

stops.name: The Capitol, the Third Annual Message
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 December 1863. The amnesty and reconstruction proclamation issued with this message is standard secondary detail, not in the research pool.
stops.campa: The national banks are chartering, the notes are circulating, and the armies are being paid on time, which nobody in 1861 would have promised. He reports to Congress that the banking law has proved a valuable support of the public credit and that no change in its principles is needed. In the same message he offers amnesty and a plan of reconstruction to any seceded state where a tenth of the voters will swear loyalty. He is arranging the peace and the currency in one document, sixteen months before the war ends.
stops.quote: Since these measures have been in operation all demands on the Treasury, including the pay of the Army and Navy, have been promptly met and fully satisfied.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Lincoln, Third Annual Message to Congress, 8 December 1863 (Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The Third Annual Message to Congress, 8 December 1863
sources: Abraham Lincoln, Third Annual Message to Congress, 8 December 1863 (Wikisource)

stops.name: Washington, the act revised and the worst month
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 June 1864 for the revised National Bank Act and to July 1864 for the worst wartime rate, 258 greenback dollars per 100 in gold, month only. Newton's 1717 ratio is attested in newton.journey.json; pairing it against the Legal Tender Act is a reconstruction, not a claim either source makes.
stops.campa: In June a revised National Bank Act supersedes the 1863 law and tightens the standards of the system. In July the paper reaches its worst: two hundred and fifty-eight greenback dollars buy one hundred dollars in gold. A hundred and forty-seven years earlier Isaac Newton, Master of the Mint, had fixed the guinea against silver at twenty-one shillings and put England accidentally onto a gold standard it kept for two centuries. The Union has cut the link Newton's ratio assumed, on purpose, and is paying for the war in the difference.
stops.quote: A return to specie payments, however, at the earliest period compatible with due regard to all interests concerned should ever be kept in view.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Lincoln, Second Annual Message to Congress, 1 December 1862 (Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The revised National Bank Act of 3 June 1864

stops.name: The Capitol, the Fourth Annual Message and the 584 banks
stops.date_confidence: attested to 6 December 1864 for the message and 25 November 1864 for the count of 584 national banks. The 10 percent tax on state bank notes is attested to 1865, effective 1866.
stops.campa: By the twenty-fifth of November five hundred and eighty-four national banks have organized, a good many of them converted state banks, and in the spring Congress will tax state bank notes at ten percent to finish the job. He tells Congress the Treasury cannot be conducted unless the government can restrain the note circulation of the country, and that he hopes soon there will be no bank of issue in the United States not authorized by Congress. This is the last annual message he writes. The system it describes outlives him by fifty years.
stops.quote: Changes from State systems to the national system are rapidly taking place, and it is hoped that very soon there will be in the United States no banks of issue not authorized by Congress and no bank-note circulation not secured by the Government.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Lincoln, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, 6 December 1864 (Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The Fourth Annual Message to Congress, 6 December 1864
sources: Abraham Lincoln, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, 6 December 1864 (Wikisource)

stops.name: Washington, reelected over McClellan
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1864; day defaults to 01. The blind memorandum of August 1864, the fall of Atlanta and the soldier vote are standard secondary detail, not in the research pool.
stops.campa: In August he writes a memorandum saying he expects to be beaten, folds it, and asks his cabinet to sign the back of it unread. Then Sherman takes Atlanta. In November he beats George McClellan, the general he had removed, running on a platform that calls the war a failure. The soldiers in the field vote for the man who has been sending them into it. No American president has been reelected in thirty-two years, and none has ever been reelected in the middle of a civil war, because there has not been one.
suggested_refs: The blind memorandum of 23 August 1864, signed unread by the cabinet

stops.name: The White House, the address from St Martin's Hall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the exchange. The founding of the International at St Martin's Hall on 28 September 1864 is attested in karl_marx.journey.json; the congratulatory address to Lincoln and Charles Francis Adams's reply on his behalf are not in that file and are not in the research pool as a dated event. The January date is approximate.
stops.campa: Four months after founding the International Working Men's Association at St Martin's Hall in London, Karl Marx drafts an address from its General Council congratulating Lincoln on his reelection and telling him the American war is the working class's war. It goes through the legation in London. Charles Francis Adams, the United States minister, answers on the President's behalf in courteous diplomatic form, which is the only reply the International ever gets from a head of state. The atlas has the London end of this already. The Washington end is here.
suggested_refs: The IWMA Address to Abraham Lincoln, drafted by Marx, and Adams's reply

stops.name: The Capitol, the second inaugural
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 March 1865. The research pool supplies no verified text of the Second Inaugural, so the campa paraphrases rather than quoting, apart from the three words carved on the memorial wall.
stops.campa: He takes the oath a second time under a dome finished during the war. The speech runs well under a thousand words and does not celebrate the coming victory. It says that both sides read the same Bible and pray to the same God, that slavery was the cause, and that the war may be the price the whole country owes for it, North and South together, however long the paying takes. Then it asks for malice toward none. Six weeks later he is dead, and the sentence is cut into the wall of his memorial.
suggested_refs: The Second Inaugural Address, 4 March 1865, inscribed in the Lincoln Memorial

stops.name: Ford's Theatre, the shot
stops.date_confidence: attested to 14 April 1865. Coordinate corrected: the research pool gave 38.8973, -77.0247, roughly 130 metres off and mid-block; Ford's Theatre at 511 10th Street NW is at 38.8967, -77.0258 per NPS and Wikipedia.
stops.campa: Five days after Appomattox, on Good Friday, the Lincolns go to Ford's Theatre on Tenth Street to see Our American Cousin. Grant has declined the invitation. The one policeman on the door of the box is not at his post. John Wilkes Booth, an actor who knows the play and knows which line gets the biggest laugh, opens the door during that line and fires a derringer ball into the back of the President's head, jumps to the stage, and goes out through wings he has walked a hundred times.
suggested_refs: Ford's Theatre, 511 10th Street NW, Washington

stops.name: The Petersen House, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the morning of 15 April 1865. Coordinate is the Petersen boarding house directly across 10th Street NW from the theatre. Stanton's words at the deathbed are recorded both ways by men who were in the room, and the disagreement is not resolved here.
stops.campa: They carry him across Tenth Street to a boarding house belonging to a tailor named Petersen and lay him diagonally across a bed too short for him, in a back room nine feet wide. He never regains consciousness. The cabinet comes, and the surgeons, and Mary is taken out weeping. He dies at twenty-two minutes past seven in the morning. Stanton says either that he now belongs to the ages or that he now belongs to the angels; the men in the room disagreed about it afterward and never settled it. He is fifty-six.
suggested_refs: The Petersen House, across 10th Street from Ford's Theatre

stops.name: The Capitol Rotunda, the funeral train sets out
stops.date_confidence: attested to a departure at 8:00 a.m. on 21 April 1865. Distance corrected: the research pool said roughly 1,700 miles; the documented figure is 1,654 miles through seven states in thirteen days. That the route retraced his 1861 inaugural journey, and that Willie's coffin travelled with him, are standard secondary detail.
stops.campa: He lies in state under the Capitol dome and then goes home the long way. The funeral train leaves Washington at eight in the morning on the twenty-first of April and takes thirteen days to cover one thousand six hundred and fifty-four miles through seven states, stopping at Baltimore, Harrisburg, Philadelphia, New York, Albany, Buffalo, Cleveland, Columbus, Indianapolis, Michigan City and Chicago. It retraces, almost exactly, the route he rode east as president-elect in 1861. The coffin of his son Willie travels with him.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln funeral train itinerary, 21 April to 3 May 1865
sources: Wikipedia, 'Funeral and burial of Abraham Lincoln'

stops.name: Oak Ridge Cemetery, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 May 1865. Coordinate corrected: the research pool gave 39.8203, -89.6501 on four separate items, roughly 600 metres off and outside the tomb grounds; the Lincoln Tomb is at 39.8233, -89.6558.
stops.campa: On the fourth of May he is buried at Oak Ridge Cemetery on the north edge of Springfield, two miles from the house on Eighth Street and from the office where Herndon has already begun asking people what they remember. Mary insisted on Oak Ridge against the town's committee, which had bought a plot downtown and built a vault for him there. The receiving vault at Oak Ridge is temporary. So is nearly every arrangement made for this body over the next thirty-six years.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln Tomb, Oak Ridge Cemetery, Springfield, Illinois
sources: Illinois Historic Preservation Agency, Lincoln Tomb records

stops.name: Lincoln Tomb, the counterfeiters
stops.date_confidence: attested to 7 November 1876, from Secret Service case records and Speer's account of the trial, both reaching this file at second hand. The engraver's name, the prison, the ransom figure and the choice of election night are standard secondary detail not in the research pool.
stops.campa: A Chicago ring of counterfeiters under Big Jim Kennally wants its engraver out of prison. The plan is to steal Lincoln's body from the unguarded tomb on election night, hide it in the dunes, and trade it for a pardon and a cash ransom. One of the gang is a Secret Service informer. Agents are waiting in the dark inside the memorial hall when the men pry the marble slab off the sarcophagus and get the lid part way up. Afterward the custodian keeps the coffin under a woodpile in the basement.
suggested_refs: The 1876 attempt on the Lincoln Tomb, Secret Service case file
sources: Secret Service case records (at second hand)
Bonnie Stahlman Speer, The Lincoln Conspiracy Trial (at second hand)

stops.name: Lincoln Tomb, the concrete vault
stops.date_confidence: attested to 26 September 1901. The seventeen movings named in the campa are retagged as tradition: documented relocations between 1865 and 1901 number closer to half a dozen, and the pool's own hedge, 'by some counts', concedes the figure. The twenty-three witnesses are standard secondary detail.
stops.campa: For twenty-five years the coffin is moved around the tomb by men acting largely on their own judgment: under the floor, into a hidden brick vault, out again for the rebuilding. Popular telling makes it seventeen movings; the documented ones are closer to half a dozen. On the twenty-sixth of September 1901, on Robert Todd Lincoln's instructions, the coffin is opened one last time so that twenty-three witnesses can look at the face and swear it is him. Then it is set in a steel cage and sunk under ten feet of concrete, where it has stayed.
suggested_refs: The 1901 reinterment of Abraham Lincoln, Oak Ridge Cemetery
sources: Illinois Historic Preservation Agency, Lincoln Tomb restoration records

stops.name: Philadelphia Mint, the Lincoln cent
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2 August 1909. No coordinate is given in the research pool; the pin is the third Philadelphia Mint building, in service in 1909. The removal and 1918 restoration of Brenner's initials, and the Brady photograph behind the portrait, are standard secondary detail.
stops.campa: For the centennial of his birth the Mint puts him on the cent, from a plaque by Victor David Brenner, a Lithuanian-born sculptor who modeled him from a photograph. It is the first circulating United States coin to carry the likeness of a real person; until now the country has used allegorical figures, on the argument that republics do not put faces on money the way monarchies do. The smallest coin in the country now carries the man who authorized its first paper money. Brenner's initials are struck off within days after complaints and put back in 1918.
suggested_refs: The 1909 VDB Lincoln cent, first circulating U.S. coin bearing a real person

stops.name: Platt Fields Park, the Lancashire statue
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1919 for the gift and erection; month and day default to 01. Place corrected: the research pool pinned Lincoln Square, but the statue stood in Platt Fields Park from 1919 and was moved into the city only in 1986. The 1862 address of the Manchester working men and Lincoln's reply are standard secondary detail.
stops.campa: Lancashire's mills ran on slave-grown cotton, and when the Union blockade cut the supply the mill towns starved. The workers of Manchester held to the blockade anyway and said so to Lincoln in a public address, which he answered. Fifty-six years later George Grey Barnard's standing bronze of him, given to the city by Mr and Mrs Charles Phelps Taft, is set up in Platt Fields Park. In 1986 it is moved into the middle of the city, and the square it stands in takes his name.
suggested_refs: George Grey Barnard's Lincoln, Manchester, erected 1919 and moved 1986
sources: Manchester City Council public monuments records

stops.name: The Lincoln Memorial, dedication and a wreath from Havana
stops.date_confidence: attested to 30 May 1922 for the dedication and April 1959 for Castro's visit, which fidel_castro.journey.json pins at the Capitol and carries as a detail inside that stop. Segregated seating at the dedication is standard secondary detail, not in the research pool.
stops.campa: Daniel Chester French seats him nineteen feet high in marble at the west end of the Mall, facing the Capitol, with the Gettysburg Address on one wall and the Second Inaugural on the other. Black guests at the dedication are seated in a separate section. In April 1959 Fidel Castro, three months into his revolution and in Washington on a public relations tour, lays a wreath at the foot of the statue and tells reporters he has read a great deal of Lincoln. He is photographed looking up at it for a long time.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln Memorial, west end of the National Mall, Washington

stops.name: Mount Rushmore, the fourth head
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1927 for the start of carving and 1941 for its completion; month and day default to 01. The Lakota name for the mountain and the broken Fort Laramie treaty are standard historical fact, not supplied by the research pool.
stops.campa: Gutzon Borglum blasts him out of granite in the Black Hills, fourth in a row with Washington, Jefferson, and Theodore Roosevelt, on a mountain the Lakota call the Six Grandfathers and hold under a treaty the United States broke for the gold in it. The work takes fourteen years and stops in 1941. The face is sixty feet from chin to hairline. He is on the cent, on the five-dollar bill, on the marble at the end of the Mall, and now on a mountain in country the United States took back after promising it away.
suggested_refs: Mount Rushmore National Memorial, Keystone, South Dakota
